name: Hair system / toupee
lead: A toupee is a hairpiece or partial wig of natural or synthetic hair worn to cover partial baldness or for theatrical purposes; the word comes from the French toupet, meaning a tuft of hair.[1] In modern hair-loss communities the term hair system usually refers to a custom-made, non-surgical hair prosthesis, typically fixed to the scalp with adhesive or tape, that replaces or fills in lost hair.[1][2]

Dermatology literature lists hairpieces among the hair camouflage options available when medical and surgical treatments are insufficient or unsuitable.[2] A 2024 case series of six patients examined hair system-induced alopecia, asking whether it arises from traction or from pressure.[3] No trial has compared hair systems with other treatments for appearance or quality of life.
On looksmaxxing forums, hair systems are discussed as one of several routes for men with hair loss, alongside drug treatment, transplantation and a shaved head.[4]

paras: Toupees are often custom-made, using synthetic or human hair.[1] In the 1950s, Max Factor-style designs sewed individual strands to fine, flesh-coloured lace so the piece looked nearly invisible.[1] Adhesive is described as the usual attachment method; an elastic band appears in cheaper versions; and hair weaving, in which the base is woven into the wearer's own hair, was popular in the 1980s and 1990s.[1]
Wear and tear is a recurring theme. Saltwater and chlorine age toupees quickly, some shampoos can damage the fibres, and pieces need periodic replacement.[1]

Toupees developed in the 18th century and lost popularity after the French Revolution; their use grew in the United States in the 19th century as men sought a younger appearance.[1] Sears sold them by mail order in 1900, and the first toupee patent was filed in 1921.[1] More than 350,000 U.S. men were estimated to wear hairpieces in the 1950s, and Time estimated over 2.5 million in 1970.[1]

Demand among men declined afterwards. Alternatives noted in the literature include comb-overs, drug treatments such as minoxidil and finasteride introduced for hair loss in the 1990s, and hair transplantation; shorter haircuts and growing acceptance of baldness are also cited.[1] A Japanese wigmaker reported new orders from male customers falling 30 percent between 2002 and 2004.[1]

No studies found testing hair systems as an appearance intervention. Related published work includes a 2022 review of hair camouflage that places hairpieces among options ranging up to scalp micropigmentation,[2] a 2024 case series of six patients with alopecia attributed to hair systems,[3] and a 2025 study of unequal NHS wig provision in the UK, which treats wigs as a medical orthotic for some patients with alopecia.[5]

The 2024 case series reports hair loss in six wearers of hair systems and examines whether traction or pressure is responsible.[3] Wikipedia notes that hair weaving can cause discomfort and traction alopecia and is therefore generally not recommended.[1]

Forum members describe hair systems as the middle option between treatment or transplantation and going bald.[4] One thread's author argues that partners often respond positively once they learn a man wears one and that a system lets a man change styles; other members of that community treat such claims sceptically.[4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hair systems are presented as a concealment option for balding men and are compared with medication, transplants and baldness.[4]

claims.claim: A hair system is a better option than being bald when treatment is not possible.
claims.believers: Proponents say a wearer appears to have hair nearly all the time and can change styles, and report that some partners reacted favourably after learning of it.[4]
claims.experts: Dermatology reviews list hairpieces as a camouflage option when other treatments are limited, but no study has measured their effect on attractiveness or social perception.[2]

claims.claim: Heavy scalp massage can restore a hairline by breaking up skull calcification.
claims.believers: A poster in a hair thread says they are trying what they call detumescence therapy, describing it as heavy scalp massage, while also calling it possibly a cope.[6]
claims.experts: No published studies support this mechanism.

card.summary: A custom non-surgical hairpiece for balding men; it covers hair loss while worn, with no trials and documented traction hair loss in some wearers.
card.note: Adhesive and weave attachments are linked to traction-type hair loss in case reports.

quick.overview:
A hair system is a custom-made hairpiece, usually attached with adhesive or tape, that covers or fills in areas of hair loss. Toupees have been sold for more than a century and remain one option alongside drugs, transplants and shaving the head.

It is a camouflage rather than a treatment: appearance changes only while it is worn, and no trial has measured its effect.
quick.mechanism: A base of fine lace or similar material carries natural or synthetic hair and is fixed to the scalp by adhesive, elastic or by weaving it into existing hair.
quick.risks: A 2024 case series reported hair loss in six hair system wearers, and weaving methods are linked to traction alopecia. Pieces need regular replacement and care; saltwater, chlorine and some shampoos damage fibres.
